title: Lexical variety versus syntactic processing load in nineteenth-century children’s and adult literature
content:
by Demei Yang, Shilong Tao

Children’s literature, written by adults for young readers, is widely assumed to be linguistically simpler than literature for adults, yet this assumption has rarely been tested along separate dimensions of complexity. We compared lexical variety and syntactic processing load in all 100 texts of two CLiC corpora: the 19th Century Children’s Literature Corpus (ChiLit, 71 texts) and the 19th Century Reference Corpus (19C, 29 adult novels). Lexical variety was measured with the Moving-Average Type-Token Ratio (MATTR) at window sizes from 50 to 1000 tokens, and syntactic processing load with mean dependency distance (MDD). Mixed-effects models treated author as a random effect and adjusted for publication year, and equivalence tests asked whether the corpora differed negligibly in MDD. Adult fiction showed greater lexical variety at broad windows (W = 500: difference = 0.022, 95% CI [0.009, 0.035]; W = 1000: 0.027 [0.013, 0.042]) but not at a 50-token window (0.005 [−0.003, 0.013]), and the broad-window contrast survived control for text length. Mean MDD was almost identical in the two corpora (2.63 vs. 2.64). Adjusted for publication year, children’s fiction had marginally longer dependencies (adult minus children’s = −0.09, 95% CI [−0.18, −0.01]), a difference that lay within a ± 0.20 equivalence bound (p = 0.007) and largely reflected sentence length. Over the century, MDD fell in both corpora, mainly because sentences grew shorter. Writers for children in this period thus narrowed the range of their vocabulary without simplifying their syntax. The findings support a dimension-specific account of audience design and show that lexical comparisons depend on the scale at which lexical variety is measured.
